title: Working from home: here to stay?
text:
When offices closed almost overnight, few people expected remote working to {1} on in such a big way. Yet for millions of employees, the kitchen table has {2} over from the office desk, and many have no intention of going back.

The benefits are easy to see. Without a daily commute, workers save time and money, and many say it is easier to get {3} with demanding tasks without the constant interruptions of an open-plan office. Employers, for their part, have been quick to {4} advantage of lower costs for office space.

But the picture is not entirely positive. Managers worry that new recruits miss out on the informal learning that happens when colleagues work side by side. Others say it has become harder to draw a clear {5} between work and home life, with emails arriving late into the evening.

{6} these concerns, many companies are now experimenting with hybrid arrangements, in which staff spend part of the week in the office. Whether this compromise will {7} the test of time remains to be seen, but the traditional nine-to-five office day looks unlikely to make a full {8}.

items.hint: Which phrasal verb with 'on' means 'become popular'?
items.explanation: 'Catch on' means to become popular or fashionable. 'Take on' means to accept work or employ someone, which does not fit.

items.hint: Look at 'over from': which verb means 'replace'?
items.explanation: 'Take over from' means to replace something or someone. 'Hand over' needs 'to' (hand over to someone), and 'give over' and 'make over' do not combine with 'from' in this sense.

items.hint: Complete the phrasal verb 'get … with something' meaning 'continue doing it'.
items.explanation: 'Get on with' a task means to start or continue working on it. 'Get by with' means to manage with limited resources, and 'get over with' is used as 'get something over with'.

items.hint: Which verb completes the expression '… advantage of something'?
items.explanation: We 'take advantage of' an opportunity. We can 'gain an advantage over' someone, but not 'gain advantage of'.

items.hint: Complete the expression 'draw a … between two things'.
items.explanation: To 'draw a line between' two things is to separate them clearly. The other nouns do not combine with 'draw' in this expression.

items.hint: Three of the options need 'to' after them. Which one doesn't?
items.explanation: 'Given these concerns' means 'considering these concerns'. 'Owing', 'due' and 'thanks' would all need 'to' (owing to, due to, thanks to).

items.hint: Complete the idiom '… the test of time'.
items.explanation: Something that 'stands the test of time' continues to be successful for a long time. 'Pass a test' is correct in general, but this idiom always uses 'stand'.

items.hint: Which noun goes with 'make a (full) …' and means 'return to popularity'?
items.explanation: To 'make a comeback' is to become popular or successful again. The other nouns do not collocate with 'make a full'.

title: Why fans stay loyal
text:
Supporting a football team is rarely a rational decision. Most fans inherit their club from a parent, and once they have chosen, they are expected to stick with it through thick and {1}. Changing teams because another club is more successful is regarded as something close to treason.

This loyalty can seem baffling to outsiders. A season ticket costs a small {2}, and the reward is often ninety minutes of frustration. Yet supporters keep coming back, and psychologists believe they know why. Belonging to a group gives people a sense of identity, something we tend to take for {3} until it is threatened.

Defeat, oddly, can strengthen that bond. Sharing disappointment with thousands of strangers is a far {4} from the lonely experience of watching at home. And when success does come, perhaps out of the {5} after decades of failure, the joy is all the greater for having been so hard-earned. Even fans who claim to have lost interest usually admit to a soft {6} for the team they grew up with.

Of course, loyalty has its limits. Supporters are increasingly unwilling to turn a {7} eye to soaring ticket prices or to owners who treat clubs purely as investments. In the {8} run, clubs that ignore their fans may discover that even the most devoted supporter has a breaking point.

items.hint: Complete the idiom meaning 'in good times and bad times'.
items.explanation: 'Through thick and thin' means in good and bad times. The idiom is fixed: none of the other adjectives can replace 'thin'.

items.hint: Which noun completes the expression 'cost a small …' meaning 'be very expensive'?
items.explanation: 'To cost a small fortune' means to be very expensive. 'Treasure' and 'wealth' do not form this expression, and a 'wage' is what you earn.

items.hint: Complete the expression 'take something for …', meaning not to appreciate it.
items.explanation: 'To take something for granted' means not to value it because you assume it will always be there.

items.hint: Which idiom means 'very different from'?
items.explanation: 'A far cry from' means very different from something. The idiom is fixed; 'a far way from' does not have this meaning.

items.hint: Complete the idiom meaning 'unexpectedly'.
items.explanation: 'Out of the blue' means suddenly and unexpectedly, like a flash of lightning from a clear sky.

items.hint: Complete the expression 'have a soft … for someone', meaning 'feel affection for'.
items.explanation: 'To have a soft spot for' someone or something means to be fond of them, often without a logical reason.

items.hint: Complete the idiom meaning 'deliberately ignore something wrong'.
items.explanation: 'To turn a blind eye to' something is to pretend not to notice it. Don't confuse it with 'turn a deaf ear', which goes with 'ear', not 'eye'.

items.hint: Complete the expression 'in the … run', meaning 'eventually'.
items.explanation: 'In the long run' means over a long period of time, eventually. The other adjectives cannot be used in this fixed phrase.

title: Will AI take your job?
text:
Few technologies have generated as much excitement, or as much anxiety, as artificial intelligence. Companies of every size have been eager to adopt it, and some have already begun to lay {1} staff whose tasks can now be automated.

For workers, AI is something of a double-{2} sword. On the one hand, it can take over repetitive tasks, leaving people free to concentrate on more interesting work. On the other, it puts thousands of jobs {3} risk, particularly in areas such as customer service and data entry.

So far, however, the technology has often {4} short of the most ambitious predictions. Several firms that rushed to replace staff with chatbots have quietly rehired people after customers complained. By and {5}, the evidence suggests that AI is better at assisting people than replacing them.

That is by no {6} a reason for complacency. The skills that employers value are changing quickly, and those who refuse to adapt may find themselves left behind. Whether AI will ultimately create more jobs than it destroys is a question on which the jury is still {7}. What seems certain is that, for the next generation of workers, using these tools will soon become second {8}.

items.hint: Which phrasal verb with 'lay' means 'dismiss workers because there is no work'?
items.explanation: 'To lay off' staff is to dismiss them, usually because there is not enough work. 'Lay out' means to arrange or to spend money.

items.hint: Complete the idiom for something that has both advantages and disadvantages.
items.explanation: 'A double-edged sword' has both good and bad effects. The idiom is fixed: 'double-sided' is a real word, but not in this expression.

items.hint: Which preposition goes with 'risk' in 'put something … risk'?
items.explanation: We put something 'at risk', meaning in danger. 'In danger' takes 'in', but 'risk' takes 'at'.

items.hint: Which verb completes '… short of expectations', meaning 'fail to reach'?
items.explanation: 'To fall short of' something means to fail to reach a standard or expectation. 'Run short of' means to have too little of something, which is a different meaning.

items.hint: Complete the fixed phrase 'by and …', meaning 'generally'.
items.explanation: 'By and large' means 'on the whole, generally'. It is a fixed phrase; 'by far' exists but means 'by a great amount'.

items.hint: Complete the phrase 'by no …', meaning 'not at all'.
items.explanation: 'By no means' means 'not at all'. 'By any chance' exists, but 'by no chance' and 'by no way' are not used.

items.hint: Complete the idiom meaning 'people have not decided yet'.
items.explanation: 'The jury is still out' means that people have not yet reached a decision about something.

items.hint: Something you do so often that it feels completely natural is 'second …'.
items.explanation: If something is 'second nature' to you, you do it easily and automatically. The expression always uses 'nature'.
